message:
feat(host): notice a dead capture worker instead of waiting out its deadline

Product 1 (new header), test 1, build 1. Nothing calls it yet; the worker it waits for does not
exist, and creating it is the step still held for a decision. The reviewer confirmed this half
is needed whichever way that decision goes, which is why it is here first.

Waiting on the worker's completion event alone is the obvious shape and is wrong twice.

A worker that dies without producing anything never signals. Killed during an update, crashed,
terminated by anything at all -- the caller would sit out the entire deadline to learn something
the OS already knew. Waiting on the process handle as well makes that answer arrive at the
moment of death: measured at 1us against a one second deadline. It also makes the CAUSE
irrelevant, which is the point -- an update stopping the helper and a crash arrive on the same
path and are charged the same.

The second wrongness is subtler and is the reason for the test that names it. A well behaved
worker writes its result, signals, and exits, which leaves BOTH handles signalled, and
WaitForMultipleObjects returns the lowest index among them. Put the process first and every
successful capture is read as a dead worker -- constantly, since exiting is what a correct
worker does. Completion is index zero for that reason and there is a check that fails if it
stops being.

Cancellation is the only outcome that costs the window nothing. A cancelled wait never asked the
window anything, so holding it against the window would punish it for the session going away.

20 checks, three consecutive clean runs. They fail for the right reasons: putting the process
handle first breaks 9, and dropping it from the wait entirely breaks 9. One case uses a real
child process rather than an event, because "a process exiting signals its handle" is what
everything else here rests on and asserting it with an event would be assuming the thing under
test.

One check started out wrong: it required the timed-out wait to have taken at least the full
deadline. A Windows wait is granular to the timer tick and came back at 198.6ms of 200ms
measured against QPC. The product was right and the assertion was not; it now carries a tick of
slack and bounds the other side too.
